item.title: Injective SDK, Braintree.Net Supply Chain Malware, GigaWiper, and UAT-7810 ORBs
item.content:encoded:
Injective SDK on npm infected with cryptocurrency wallet stealer — Should Read

Hackers compromised Injective Labs’ GitHub repository to publish malicious npm versions of its SDK and related packages that stole crypto wallet private keys and seed phrases when wallet functions were used. Developers who installed the affected version should assume wallets and secrets may be compromised, move funds to new wallets, and rotate credentials.

  • Hackers compromised a GitHub account belonging to a legitimate Injective Labs SDK project contributor and used it to publish malicious version 1.20.21 of the @injectivelabs/sdk-ts npm package.
  • The malicious package stole cryptocurrency wallet private keys and mnemonic seed phrases when developers used SDK functions that generate or import wallet keys.
  • The attacker also published version 1.20.21 for 17 other packages associated with the project, pinning all of them to the compromised SDK version.
  • Socket reported that the malicious package version was downloaded 310 times before it was deprecated, and Ox Security warned that 87 dependent packages had a cumulative download count of just over 112,000.
  • The legitimate account owner detected the compromise within minutes, reverted the changes, and published a clean release, version 1.20.23.

Fake Braintree NuGet Package Skims Credit Cards and Harvests Merchant Credentials — Should Read

A malicious NuGet typosquat, Braintree.Net, impersonated PayPal Braintree’s official SDK while stealing live payment card data, Braintree merchant API keys, and host secrets through a companion DependencyInjector.Core package. Any organization that used the affected packages should remove them, rotate credentials, investigate possible card-data exposure, and block the attacker domain.

  • Socket’s AI scanner flagged a malicious NuGet package named Braintree.Net that masqueraded as PayPal Braintree’s official .NET SDK and routed stolen data to api.348672-shakepay[.]com.
  • Confirmed malicious Braintree.Net versions 3.35.8 through 3.36.1 intercepted live payment card data, including full card numbers, CVVs, expiration dates, customer IDs, amounts, operations, gateways, card types, and timestamps.
  • The typosquat stole Braintree merchant credentials by sending merchantId, publicKey, and privateKey values to the attacker endpoint when a production gateway was configured.
  • Starting with Braintree.Net 3.36.0, the package depended on DependencyInjector.Core, which used module initializers to collect environment variables, appsettings JSON contents, cloud and container metadata, dependencies, and loaded assemblies on assembly load.
  • Socket recommended removing Braintree.Net, replacing it with the official Braintree package, rotating Braintree merchant credentials, auditing for DependencyInjector.Core, SipNet, and SipNet.OpenAI.Realtime, and hunting for outbound POSTs to api.348672-shakepay[.]com.

New GigaWiper Windows Backdoor Bundles Disk Wiping, Fake Ransomware, and Spyware — Should Read

Microsoft analyzed GigaWiper, a Windows backdoor also tracked as BLUERABBIT, that combines spying and remote-control features with multiple destructive wipers disguised partly as ransomware. Defenders should focus on early detection and offline backups because once deployed, the malware can irreversibly destroy systems rather than enable recovery or ransom payment.

  • Microsoft analyzed a destructive Windows backdoor called GigaWiper that combines three older destructive programs into operator-selectable commands.
  • The same malicious files are tracked by Binary Defense as BLUERABBIT, and both reports list the same four hashes and matching command servers.
  • GigaWiper can wipe the physical drive, run fake ransomware based on Crucio that encrypts files without saving a key, or overwrite the Windows drive using a Go rewrite of FlockWiper.
  • The backdoor can also take screenshots, record the screen, open a hidden VNC session, collect system details, manage programs and services, edit the registry, and wipe Windows event logs.
  • Microsoft recommends watching for signals such as a recurring OneDrive Update scheduled task, RabbitMQ or Redis traffic from ordinary desktops, and processes using takeown and icacls on Windows boot files outside maintenance windows.

Dormant GitHub Accounts Help Attackers Blend In While Mapping Corporate Orgs — Should Read

Datadog Security Labs warns that attackers are using years-old dormant GitHub “ghost” accounts and compromised tokens to quietly enumerate corporate GitHub orgs, repos, and users via the GitHub API. Most activity targets public data for reconnaissance, but some cases escalated to cloning private repositories.

  • Datadog Security Labs warned of several overlapping campaigns systematically enumerating corporate GitHub organizations, repositories, and user accounts through the GitHub API.
  • The operators use automated scraping tools with custom or legitimate-sounding user agents, GitHub “ghost” accounts that are often years old, and compromised OAuth tokens or personal access tokens from legitimate users.
  • More than 50 dormant accounts and dozens of legitimate accounts with exposed or compromised personal access tokens were used to facilitate the enumeration.
  • The GitHub “ghost” accounts were created two to five years ago and left inactive for long periods before being used to issue API traffic across multiple organizations.
  • Most activity involved public data, but Datadog confirmed a few scenarios where attackers went beyond enumeration and cloned a private repository belonging to a single organization.

WolfSSL, GeoVision, VTK vulnerabilities — Optional

Cisco Talos disclosed and coordinated patches for vulnerabilities in WolfSSL, GeoVision, and VTK-DICOM, including input validation, command injection, buffer overflow, privilege escalation, and authentication issues. The largest impact is GeoVision, with 14 advisories covering 37 CVEs.

  • Cisco Talos’ Vulnerability Discovery & Research team disclosed three vulnerabilities in WolfSSL, fourteen in GeoVision, and one in VTK-DICOM.
  • The vulnerabilities discussed in the article have been patched by their respective vendors in line with Cisco’s third-party vulnerability disclosure policy.
  • The WolfSSL issues include two improper input validation vulnerabilities, TALOS-2026-2409 and TALOS-2026-2410, and one integer underflow vulnerability, TALOS-2026-2408.
  • Talos released 14 advisories for GeoVision vulnerabilities, covering 37 CVEs across issues such as memory corruption, OS command injection, buffer overflows, privilege escalation, reflected XSS, insufficient encryption, and lack of authentication.
  • Talos found one VTK-DICOM vulnerability, TALOS-2026-2366, tracked as CVE-2026-22879, which is a heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability.

Winning 54% of the time — Optional

Cisco Talos reports that China-nexus actor UAT-7810 is expanding covert Operational Relay Box networks by exploiting unpatched Ruckus and ASUS routers and deploying custom backdoors like LONGLEASH and DOGLEASH. Defenders should prioritize patching edge devices and monitoring for unusual proxying or unauthorized connections.

  • Cisco Talos reported that the China-nexus threat actor UAT-7810 is expanding its Operational Relay Box networks with a new suite of custom malware.
  • UAT-7810 exploits known vulnerabilities in unpatched Ruckus and ASUS routers to deploy tools including upgraded LONGLEASH and DOGLEASH backdoors.
  • Talos says UAT-7810 builds covert networks to provide infrastructure for other APT groups to launch attacks against high-value targets.
  • The article states that ORB networks allow secondary threat actors to mask their origins and route malicious traffic through seemingly innocuous nodes.
  • Defenders are advised to fully patch edge devices, particularly Ruckus and ASUS routers, and monitor for unusual proxying behavior or unauthorized connections.

Why Do F1 Teams Need Cybersecurity, and How Is AI Changing the Threat Landscape? — Optional

F1 teams face enterprise-grade cyber risks because their competitive advantage depends on fast-moving telemetry, software, partner access, and global operations. The article argues that AI is making phishing, deepfakes, and discovery faster for attackers, while zero trust and AI-driven security controls are needed to protect data, identities, vendors, and AI systems.

  • Formula 1 teams generate hundreds of gigabytes of telemetry across a race weekend, and this data moves between the car, garage, trackside systems, factory, and pit wall.
  • The article says F1 teams must protect live telemetry, proprietary software and analytics, business data, and global operations across more than 20 countries in a season.
  • Third-party vendors, suppliers, contractors, media, and sponsors can extend an F1 team’s attack surface because they may need temporary or integrated access to systems.
  • The article identifies IP theft, ransomware, and social engineering as key threats facing F1 teams, with race timing increasing pressure during outages.
  • The article states that AI can help attackers create convincing phishing content, deepfakes, and automated discovery campaigns, while also helping defenders baseline normal behavior and correlate risks.
